text: Then the high priest asked, "Are these charges true?"
And Stephen said: "Brothers and fathers, listen to me. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he settled in Haran,
and said to him, 'Leave your country and your kindred, and go to the land I will show you.'
So he left the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. And after his father died, God moved him to this land where you are now living.
He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot of ground, yet he promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his descendants after him, though at the time he had no child.
And God said this: his descendants would live as strangers in a foreign land, and they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.

versions.text: God said this to him: that his descendants would live as strangers in a foreign land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
versions.explanation: The Greek has no "to him" (ἐλάλησεν οὕτως ὁ θεὸς = "God spoke in this way"), and the construction "said this to him: that... and that..." is clumsy when read aloud. The revised wording is both closer to the Greek and smoother for oral reading.

text: 'But I will judge the nation they serve,' God said, 'and afterward they will come out and worship me in this place.'
And God gave him the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; and Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob of the twelve patriarchs.
"The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. But God was with him,
and rescued him from all his troubles. He gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who made him ruler over Egypt and over all his household.
Then a famine came over all Egypt and Canaan, bringing great hardship, and our fathers could find no food.
When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there on a first visit.
On their second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned of Joseph's family.
Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five people in all.
So Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our fathers died.
Their bodies were brought back to Shechem and laid in the tomb that Abraham had bought for a sum of silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
"As the time drew near for the promise God had made to Abraham, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
until another king rose to power over Egypt who knew nothing of Joseph.
He dealt treacherously with our people and oppressed our fathers, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would not survive.
At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful in God's sight. For three months he was raised in his father's house,
and when he was abandoned, Pharaoh's daughter took him and brought him up as her own son.
So Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in his words and deeds.
When he was forty years old, he decided to visit his brothers, the people of Israel.
Seeing one of them being wronged, he came to his defense and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian.
He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to bring them deliverance, but they did not.
The next day he came upon two of them fighting and tried to reconcile them, saying, 'Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging each other?'
But the one who was wronging his neighbor pushed him aside and said, 'Who made you ruler and judge over us?
Do you mean to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'
At this word Moses fled and lived as a stranger in the land of Midian, where he became the father of two sons.
"Forty years later an angel appeared to him in the wilderness near Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. And as he drew near to look, the voice of the Lord came to him:

versions.text: When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight. As he went closer to look, he heard the voice of the Lord:
versions.explanation: The Greek is impersonal (ἐγένετο φωνὴ κυρίου, "a voice of the Lord came"), not "he heard"; keeping the voice as the subject preserves the emphasis of the original and flows well aloud.

text: 'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob.' Moses began to tremble and dared not look.
Then the Lord said to him, 'Take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have surely seen the oppression of my people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to set them free. Now come, I will send you to Egypt.'
"This Moses, whom they rejected with the words, 'Who made you ruler and judge?'—this is the man God sent as both ruler and redeemer, by the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
He led them out, performing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.

versions.text: He led them out, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
versions.explanation: The Greek reads ἐν γῇ Αἰγύπτῳ, "in the land of Egypt"; restoring "the land of" matches the original and gives the triple phrase a fuller rhythm for reading aloud.

text: This is the Moses who said to the people of Israel, 'God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.'
He is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers; and he received living words to pass on to us.
But our fathers refused to obey him. They rejected him and in their hearts turned back to Egypt,
saying to Aaron, 'Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we have no idea what has become of him.'
In those days they made a calf, offered a sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their own hands.

versions.text: In those days they made a calf, brought a sacrifice to the idol, and celebrated the work of their own hands.
versions.explanation: ἀνήγαγον θυσίαν is the standard idiom for "offered a sacrifice" rather than "brought"; and εὐφραίνοντο ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις is "rejoiced in the works" (plural), which better conveys their delight in their idolatrous handiwork.

text: So God turned away and gave them over to the worship of the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: 'Did you bring me sacrifices and offerings for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
No, you carried the tent of Molech and the star of the god Rephan, the images you made to worship. So I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'

versions.text: No, you carried the tent of Molech and the star of your god Rephan, the images you made to worship. So I will send you into exile beyond Babylon.'
versions.explanation: The base text reads simply "the god Rephan" without the possessive pronoun; "your" reflects a different manuscript reading and adds content not in the text being translated.

text: "Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, made just as the one who spoke to Moses directed, according to the pattern he had seen.

versions.text: "Our fathers had the tent of testimony in the wilderness, made just as God directed when he spoke to Moses, according to the pattern he had seen.
versions.explanation: The Greek uses the participial phrase "the one who spoke to Moses" rather than naming God; preserving the original phrasing keeps the reverent circumlocution of Stephen's speech while remaining clear and readable.

text: Our fathers who followed them brought it with them under Joshua when they took possession of the land from the nations God drove out before them. And it remained until the days of David,
who found favor with God and asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob.
But it was Solomon who built him a house.
Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says:
'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool for my feet. What kind of house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what place is there for my rest?
Has not my own hand made all these things?'
"You stubborn people, uncircumcised in heart and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit—just as your fathers did, so do you.
Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One, and now you have betrayed and murdered him—
you who received the law delivered by angels, and did not keep it."
When they heard this, they were enraged in their hearts and ground their teeth at him.
But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at God's right hand.
"Look," he said, "I see heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
But they screamed at the top of their voices, covered their ears, and rushed at him with one accord.

versions.text: At this they covered their ears and, shouting at the top of their voices, rushed at him with one accord.
versions.explanation: The Greek sequence is: they cried out, covered their ears, then rushed at him. Restoring that order gives a cleaner, more forceful line for oral reading and avoids the embedded participial clause that interrupts the rhythm.

text: They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile the witnesses laid their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.
And as they stoned him, Stephen called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."

Then he fell to his knees and cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And with these words he fell asleep.[^1]

[^1]: "Fell asleep" is a gentle way of saying he died.

versions.text: Then he fell to his knees and cried out with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And with these words he fell asleep.
versions.explanation: The idiom "fell asleep" for death is worth a brief footnote so that hearers unfamiliar with the expression do not misunderstand; the verse text itself needs no change.
